summary: The customer evidence is thin: four outside conversations, all with engineers, none with a buyer, and none of VSI's 88 signals validated. What it does show is sharp. On the publishing side the time goes into getting a correct change approved, not into writing it: one public-API developer says a change takes two to three weeks of review while the writing takes seconds (E4). One engineering lead says most APIs have no usable spec to generate from (E4). The consumer side rests on web data, where agents now read most docs traffic and still fail most real tasks. Both point where the vision board does: prove that tasks still pass and take a review step away, before generating more surfaces. Next, talk to ten people who own an API budget.

icps.name: Public API owner, release side
icps.segment: Companies whose external REST API serves paying clients and partners, mid-size to large
icps.who: Backend and platform teams who ship spec changes, and the platform or API product lead who answers for what clients see.
icps.trigger: A spec change is merged and has to reach docs, tooling and clients without breaking integrations pinned to older versions.
jobs: Get a correct change approved and published in days, not weeks
Decide whether a change is a fix or a breaking change, and for whom
Keep docs, tutorials and tooling in step with the spec for every version
icps.notes: The E4 pains come from one backend developer at one large commerce SaaS, who says he is not a decider. No platform lead, API product manager, DevRel lead or technical writer has been interviewed, although the plan names them as the ICP. Copy reviewers who approve spec wording are a stakeholder the plan does not name.

icps.name: Engineering lead with unspecced APIs
icps.segment: Corporate and mid-size engineering teams whose APIs grew without OpenAPI and must now serve partners or the public
icps.who: Senior developers who set the team's tooling rules, keep docs as Markdown in Git and would rather build a tool than buy one.
icps.trigger: An internal tool has to become a public or partner API, with the versioning, structure and docs it never had.
jobs: Find out how far the APIs are from a usable spec
Retrofit structure and versioning without a week of senior time
Adopt tooling that runs inside the company's own infrastructure
icps.notes: One engineering lead, E3 to E4. His estimate that 90% of teams lack a usable spec is not a measurement; the board's first move counts it on the 200-company target list. He requires in-VPN deployment, which one voice cannot yet make a segment rule.

icps.name: Integrating developer and coding agent
icps.segment: Developers at client and partner companies, and the coding agents they direct, building on someone else's API
icps.who: The people and agents who read the docs, pick a surface and write the integration. They feel the failure but do not pay Doctorine.
icps.trigger: A task needs a third-party API, or an API version they pinned changes under them.
jobs: Get a working integration on the first attempt
Use the surface that costs the fewest tokens and retries
Keep the integration working when the API changes
icps.notes: No integrator was interviewed as such: the E3 signals come from producers describing their clients and from two engineers. Web data carries this journey. Treated as the source of proof for the API owner, not as a buyer, as the vision board parks the consumer kit.

journeys.title: From spec change to a release clients can use
journeys.question: Can a check on the pull request replace a review layer instead of adding one, and get a change out in days?

asis.text: An agent writes the spec and code change in seconds, supervised by the developer
Several teams edit the same spec, so a change needs coordination before it is ready

pains.text: One spec, many teams: every change needs collaboration between developers first

quotes.text: We do it all by AI and AI agents. So the actual work is nothing. So it is done free in just seconds if we know what to do.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: the APIs are not dedicated to only one team or one developer, then the changes applied to that spec needs collaborations between the devs.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: Run the agent task suite on the pull request that changes the spec, before any human looks
ideas.why: Writing now costs nothing, so the first check should be automatic too

tobe.text: The spec pull request opens and Doctorine rebuilds every surface and runs the task suite

asis.text: Date-based versions every quarter: fixes are backported, breaking changes go to a new version
Consumers are external companies, so consistency matters more than for internal teams

pains.text: Hard to tell a fix from a breaking change, such as a tax fix that alters client reports
87.3% of API versions that broke something deprecated nothing first, in a study of 2,224 specs
60% of API teams version their APIs but only 26% use semantic versioning (Postman 2025)

quotes.text: sometimes it is very hard to decide if this this change is a bug fix or a breaking change.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: The consumers of our APIs for the company that I'm working in is not the developers inside the company, but the external clients and the external companies.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: Label each change as fix or breaking and list the pinned versions and clients it affects
ideas.why: The call's clearest E4 pain, and the first of the change-review rules

tobe.text: The gate labels the change and names the versions and consumers it touches

asis.text: Developers review, ask other models to review, then QA calls the APIs by hand in Postman
Copy or content specialists sign off the wording before the spec pull request can merge

pains.text: One change takes two to three weeks to reach the docs site, spent in review, not writing
Company terminology rules for external wording are checked by hand, in several layers
A tool that adds pull requests to review per language will not be used

quotes.text: it may take 2, 3 weeks for a single change to be published in the website, in our documentation website.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: So if it's like If it needs more reviews, more PR reviews, and more time and money, then it won't work for us.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: Show on the pull request which checks passed, so a reviewer can skip a step they do today
ideas.why: The only buyable version: it must remove a review, never add one

ideas.text: Terminology and wording rules that flag only the lines a copy reviewer must read
ideas.why: Pre-answers the judgement calls that stretch review into weeks

tobe.text: Reviewers approve from the flagged items; everything else has already passed

asis.text: The spec renders in a hosted docs vendor; hand-written Markdown tutorials ship beside it
Some endpoints go live but stay out of the docs until a target client has tested them

pains.text: Tutorials go stale and point at an old version while the spec itself is current
Live endpoints are hidden from the docs for months, so the spec is not the whole truth
Outdated docs are the top collaboration blocker, named by 55% of API teams (Postman 2025)

quotes.text: For sure, the OpenAPI spec will be updated automatically, but we will live with existing outdated tutorials
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: Although the public API themselves are published, but somehow invisible from the documents.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: Yeah, it is a source of truth, but maybe not the whole truth.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: List every tutorial that references an operation the change touched
ideas.why: Folds the stale-tutorial pain into the gate instead of a writing agent

ideas.text: Staged or partner-only visibility for endpoints that are live but not yet public
ideas.why: Deliberate hiding is a manual workaround today

tobe.text: Only surfaces that passed are published, with a receipt; held-back ones are listed

asis.text: Clients pin a different version per API and integrate from the rendered portal
The docs vendor's MCP server only reads docs; no SDK, CLI or action MCP is offered

pains.text: Clients still send many questions to the team despite a polished portal
An SDK that tracks the latest spec would change behaviour for clients on pinned versions

quotes.text: they had a lot of questions asking us It seems like that document was not human-readable enough for them.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: And once the SDK upgraded based on the API spec upgrades, then that would cause some unwanted behavioral changes.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: For the access part, no. This MCP is just for the documentation.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: Report which client tasks agents fail on the owner's API, and what caused each failure
ideas.why: Integration failures are invisible to the owner today

tobe.text: Task success per surface and per version is tracked after every release

asis.text: Affected customers hear of a rollback by email or a call from the account team
Each surface that must be kept current costs a person to maintain

pains.text: No clear way to tell external consumers about an update or a rollback
Keeping a CLI and an SDK current is seen as one person each

quotes.text: Then how is the update mechanism and how are we conveying it to our external, uh, consumers?
quotes.who: Engineer, large e-commerce platform with partner APIs

quotes.text: So for the CLI front, I need one person. For the SDK front, I need one person to keep everything updated out there.
quotes.who: Engineer, large e-commerce platform with partner APIs

ideas.text: Roll back every surface together in one step, with a changelog entry for consumers
ideas.why: Rollback communication is an E3 pain no current capability covers

tobe.text: A rollback reverts docs, CLI, MCP and SDKs as one release and tells consumers what changed

journeys.title: From an unspecced API to a first verified release
journeys.question: Is spec repair, not generation, the way in for teams whose APIs were never specced?

stages.name: An API has to go public

asis.text: Internal APIs are unversioned; a new version simply replaces the old path
The pain arrives once, when an internal tool must serve outside consumers

pains.text: Making one internal tool public took a two-week retrofit of every API

quotes.text: one of the internal tools, we had to make it public. So now we have to go through the pain of going through all of the APIs
quotes.who: Engineering lead, corporate platform team

quotes.text: it was like a 2-week turnaround where we kind of went ahead and banged our head against the codebase and fixed it.
quotes.who: Engineering lead, corporate platform team

ideas.text: Offer the spec report when a team scopes a public or partner API
ideas.why: The trigger is rare but sharp; the rest of the time nobody looks

tobe.text: The team points Doctorine at the repository the day the API is scoped to go public

asis.text: Many APIs have no OpenAPI spec, structure or docs; they work and return data

pains.text: Most APIs are not OpenAPI compatible, so generation tools do not apply at all
Teams claim a usable spec they do not have, then decline for that reason
17.2% of specs in the largest public OpenAPI directory are invalid (688 of 3,992)

ideas.why: Measures the input before asking for any commitment

asis.text: A senior engineer retrofits with a coding agent and checks its output by hand

Nobody touches legacy code unless they are forced to
Automated spec repair lifted MCP generation from 76% to 94.2% of tools on 80 real contracts

quotes.text: you need a highly capable engineer that understands what Cloud Code does and what the OpenAPI spec is, because AI always lies to you.

quotes.text: No, nobody touches legacy code unless they need to.
quotes.who: Engineering lead, corporate platform team

quotes.text: Even better, give me a button that I can click and it raises a PR directly and says, hey, I fixed your crappy code, merge this

ideas.text: One repair pull request with the mechanical fixes, judgement calls left as review comments
ideas.why: The one concrete entry product a practitioner asked for

tobe.text: The team merges a repair pull request instead of spending a senior engineer's week

asis.text: Code and docs live as Markdown in Git; anything outside Git does not exist
The lead builds his own tools when he can, as he did with an AI pull request reviewer

pains.text: Would not go out of his way for an SDK or CLI, only take it if it comes automatically

ideas.text: Start on the spec and docs the team already has, as a GitHub Action, with no portal move
ideas.why: A no-migration start removes the heaviest first ask

tobe.text: The trial starts as a check on the team's own repository, not as a new portal

asis.text: Corporate tools run inside the company VPN with its own LLM keys, on an annual licence

pains.text: Hosted SaaS is a hard blocker where every tool must run inside the company's network
It must be configurable enough that the buyer never has to develop for it

quotes.text: I get your tool, I deploy it in my own virtual machine inside the VPN, and I just copy paste my secret key

asis.text: Static analysis and an AI reviewer already run on every pull request before a human

quotes.text: So static code, AI review, only at the 3rd step do you have a human that intervenes and looks at the code.

tobe.text: Every later spec change passes the gate before the new version reaches anyone

journeys.title: From a task to a working integration
journeys.question: Will failed agent tasks, shown to the API owner with their cause, be the reason the owner acts?

stages.name: Find the API and its docs

asis.text: Coding agents fetch docs at task time and prefer Markdown and llms.txt routes
Agents made 66% of traffic on one large docs platform by July 2026

pains.text: When the agent misses the skill file, it falls back to reading all the docs again
In one vendor's evals the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases

quotes.text: if the agent by some means misses that there's a SCILMD file, then you are going to basically read the docs again.
quotes.who: Engineer, large e-commerce platform with partner APIs

ideas.text: Test whether agents find and use each surface, not only whether it exists
ideas.why: Static readiness scores are free from four vendors and disagree

tobe.text: The eval records which surface each agent found and whether it used it

asis.text: Developers read the rendered reference and tutorials; agents read whatever they can fetch

pains.text: Docs are not updated after later changes, so they stop reflecting the system
Pasting a major API's docs into an agent gave 90% HTML and 10% content, per a writer

quotes.text: Let's say 3 months later we need to make an adjustment to the feature. We just do it and we don't update the documents usually.
quotes.who: Frontend engineer, mid-size consumer platform, internal API consumer

ideas.text: Name the exact page, schema or missing example behind each failed task
ideas.why: Turns a failure into a fix the owner can act on

tobe.text: Each failure points to the page or schema that caused it, in the owner's report

asis.text: Agents write their own client from the spec or call a CLI; SDKs are used where they exist

pains.text: Language SDKs look like overkill when an agent can write the calling code itself
30 MCP tools cost about 3,600 tokens a turn, used or not, per an HN builder

quotes.text: it's not expensive for them to ask agents to look at the OpenAPI spec and write the code for themselves.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

quotes.text: CLI, yeah, today when we use it with AI agents, that could be much more efficient.
quotes.who: Backend developer, multi-country commerce SaaS with a public API

ideas.text: Run the same tasks through docs, CLI, MCP and SDK and publish pass rate and tokens
ideas.why: Evidence leans CLI for agents; prove it before leading with it

tobe.text: Consumers get a CLI with JSON output and a curated MCP server; SDKs on request

asis.text: The agent writes the integration and runs it; bad docs show up as plausible wrong answers

pains.text: GPT-5 solved 43.7% of real MCP tasks; open models under 40% of web API integration tasks
On bad docs an agent throws no error; it answers anyway with what it hallucinates

ideas.text: Five real tasks per API, two agents, three runs each, with repeat agreement measured
ideas.why: A gate is only possible if results do not flip between runs

tobe.text: The same tasks run on every release, so a broken integration is caught before clients

asis.text: Consumers pin versions per API and upgrade when they are forced to

pains.text: Schema drift between backend and frontend types goes unnoticed until a user hits it
An internal SDK falls out of date with the API it wraps
Spec and live API drift costs 30 to 60 minutes in devtools per UI breakage, per an HN dev

quotes.text: it has happened that this stuff goes unnoticed and a user runs into a problem.
quotes.who: Frontend engineer, mid-size consumer platform, internal API consumer

quotes.text: it reminded me of the times that we had issues with SDK being out of date.
quotes.who: Frontend engineer, mid-size consumer platform, internal API consumer

ideas.text: Rerun consumers' tasks against every new version before it ships
ideas.why: Staleness and drift lead the market's counted complaints

tobe.text: Consumers see a last-verified mark on each surface and version

decisions.title: Lead with the agent task eval on the docs a team already has
decisions.why: Nobody asked for more surfaces: the one publisher calls the writing work nothing, generation is given away and static scores are free. A failed task on a team's own API is both the proof and the opener. Demand is untested, so settle it on the first 30 reports.

decisions.title: The gate must replace a review step, never add one
decisions.why: Two to three weeks of review per change is the only E4 publisher pain, and the same developer said a tool that adds pull requests to review will not be used. Ask every buyer which step the checks would let them skip.

decisions.title: Where there is no usable spec, open a repair pull request first
decisions.why: Unspecced APIs are an E4 pain and the repair button is the only entry product a practitioner asked for. The 90% estimate is one person's, so count usable specs on the target list before building.

decisions.title: CLI and a curated MCP first; SDKs on request and pinned per version
decisions.why: A generated SDK that follows the latest spec would break clients pinned to older versions (E3), and the CLI is the surface named for agents (E2). Let the eval's surface comparison confirm it.

decisions.title: Start in the team's own repository and hold self-hosting until two buyers ask
decisions.why: In-VPN deployment is an E4 constraint from one corporate lead. A GitHub Action on the existing spec, with outputs the team owns, avoids both a portal migration and building self-hosting too early.
